title: How To Make Deeper Connections With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an advanced, optional layer of rapport-building that goes beyond the standard SCM relationship-building tenets he has already covered in his books. He stresses that this deeper connection only works once a teacher has a genuinely solid classroom management foundation, since without it the strategy is unlikely to succeed. The core method is cultivating real empathy — not just imagining how a student might feel, but actually tuning into a student's temperament, energy, and worldview. He offers three specific techniques: mimicking a student's individual energy, tapping into one's own inner child to reach a similar developmental vantage point, and retaining a stable sense of self that allows a teacher to meet students where they are. He describes the payoff as a level of trust where students drop their usual defenses and become fully honest, calling this the power of true empathy, and frames it as most valuable with the most challenging, hard-to-reach students.
points: Deeper connection is optional and only effective once a teacher has an established, solid classroom management foundation.
The core strategy is real empathy: tuning into a student's actual temperament and worldview rather than just imagining their feelings.
Mimicking a student's individual energy level can create a subtle, comfortable sense of being 'in the pocket' together.
Tapping into one's own inner child helps a teacher reach the same developmental vantage point as the student.
The payoff is students dropping their usual defenses — averted eyes, closed body language, dishonesty — and speaking honestly.
quotes: Here at SCM, we believe building influential relationships with students is critical—for many reasons. Not the least of which is that it makes everything, especially managing behavior, easier.
Otherwise, if you haven’t reached this level of expertise and consistency, the strategy is unlikely to work. You must have a strong foundation before going deeper and more influential.
I mean actually dropping into their wavelength of temperament, vitality, and worldview, which can open a door of influence to a whole other level.

It’s subtle, but something you can notice within each of your students. By just being aware of it, and adjusting to it, you can slowly begin mimicking their individual energy when you interact with them.
You know you’re on the right track when you speak to students and all their usual defenses—averted eyes, closed body language, tight lips, dishonesty, etc.—are gone.
Making deeper connections with students takes strong observational powers, which is a characteristic of great teaching. It takes forgetting yourself completely and focusing on your students.
